opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, it's a great question, and I think the honest answer is that the limits are real but they're more nuanced than the headlines suggest.

The core issue is that a model's synthetic output is essentially a sample from its own learned distribution. If you naively train on that and repeat the loop, you tend to lose the tails. The rare, weird, interesting stuff gets underrepresented each round, and you converge toward a blander, more homogenous version of the data. People call that model collapse. In images you see it pretty clearly: diversity drops, certain styles or compositions start to dominate, and artifacts can get reinforced instead of corrected.

But I don't think that means synthetic data is a dead end. It depends on what you're adding to the loop. If the synthetic data is just the model talking to itself with no new signal, you're mostly recycling information it already has. If there's some external source of truth, like a verifier, a human preference, a physics simulator, a filter that's better than the generator, or real data mixed back in, then you're injecting new information and you can actually improve. The selection step is where the value comes from.

So the way I frame it is: synthetic data is great for reshaping what a model knows. You can rebalance it, make it more consistent, teach it a format, distill a big model into a smaller one, or fill in coverage for cases that are rare in the real world. It's much weaker at creating knowledge that wasn't there to begin with.

In practice, I'd say a few things matter a lot. Keep real data in the mix and don't let it get washed out. Be really deliberate about measuring diversity, not just quality, because it's easy to optimize for polished outputs and not notice you've narrowed the distribution. And treat curation and filtering as first-class research problems, because that's really where the leverage is.

So limits, yes. But I see it less as a hard wall and more as a question of where the new information is coming from.

r002.rationale: It explicitly describes synthetic-data effects in images, including reduced diversity and reinforced artifacts, connecting the text-focused training question to the image domain.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, it's a question I get asked a lot, and I think the honest answer is that it depends enormously on what you mean by "its own." There's a version of this that's genuinely concerning, and there's a version that's actually how a lot of progress gets made right now.

The concerning version is the closed loop. You take a generative model, you sample from it, you train the next model on those samples, and you repeat. What happens is pretty well understood at this point. The model is a lossy compression of the data distribution. It's going to undersample the tails, overweight the modes, and each generation you lose a little bit of the diversity you started with. People call it model collapse. In images you see it very visibly, things get smoother, more homogeneous, textures start to look the same. In language you get this kind of flattening of style. So if the question is "can a model bootstrap itself indefinitely from nothing but its own outputs," I think the answer is no, and I don't think that's controversial anymore.

But that framing misses where most of the actual value is. Synthetic data works when there's some source of signal that isn't the model itself. That can be a verifier, like in code or math where you can run the thing and check whether the answer is right. It can be a human in the loop doing selection or editing. It can be a stronger model distilling into a weaker one. Or in the vision world, it can be a renderer, a physics simulator, something that encodes real structure about the world that the model doesn't already have. In all those cases you're not really training on the model's own data, you're training on the model's data filtered or shaped by something external. And that external thing is doing the heavy lifting.

The way I think about it is that synthetic data is a great way to move information around, and a bad way to create it. If you have a filter, a reward, a simulator, that's a source of information, and the model is just the thing that proposes candidates. If you don't have that, you're just reshuffling what the model already knows, and usually losing some of it in the process.

The other limit I'd flag is more subtle. Even with a good filter, you're sampling from the model's prior. So you'll get a lot of data in the regions the model already finds easy to generate, and very little in the regions it finds hard. That's exactly backwards from what you'd want. So there's a real question of coverage. You can fix some of it with prompting, with diversity objectives, with deliberately seeking out failure cases. But it never fully goes away, and I think that's where real data, messy, long-tail, human-generated data, continues to matter for a long time.

r001.rationale: The response mentions human selection or editing as one source of signal, but does not say that the balance between human and synthetic supervision remains an open question.

r002.rationale: It describes model collapse in both images and language, showing that the concern about training on synthetic outputs also applies in the image domain.

astra-6.text:
I think the key question is: where does the new information come from? If you take a model, sample its outputs, and train on those outputs indiscriminately, you’re not necessarily giving it any new signal. You can reinforce its mistakes, and you can lose some of the diversity that was in the original data. Things that are rare become even rarer as you repeat that process.

But I wouldn’t conclude that synthetic data is inherently limited or unhelpful. If you can generate a solution and then check it—say, by executing code or testing it in an environment—you have a signal beyond the model’s own confidence. That lets you select examples that are actually useful. The model might produce a correct answer only occasionally, but training on those verified answers can make that behavior more reliable.

So I’d distinguish between a model just recycling its own beliefs and a system using generation to explore, with some independent way to evaluate what it finds. Synthetic data can be very powerful in that second setting. The limitation is really the quality and coverage of the feedback: what can you verify, and what mistakes is your verifier going to miss?

sol-6.1.text:
I think the key question is where the new information is coming from. If you sample from a model and then train it on those samples, you’re not necessarily adding knowledge. You may just be reinforcing the model’s existing biases and losing some of the diversity in the original data. Rare cases can disappear, and mistakes can become more entrenched.

But I wouldn’t take that to mean synthetic data isn’t useful. If you can check the outputs against something outside the model—execute code, verify a solution, or get feedback from an environment—then you have a way to select examples that actually help. You can also use synthetic data to make existing knowledge easier to learn.

So I’d distinguish generating more text from generating a useful learning signal. The limit is less about whether the data is synthetic and more about whether there’s a reliable source of feedback that keeps the process grounded.
